tldr: The authors introduce FineART, a massive bimanual manipulation dataset with dense subtask annotations across all 1,718 hours of trajectories, and FineART-VLA, a single unified policy that predicts its own next subtask in language while generating continuous actions. Mid-training with this approach substantially improves spatial grounding and long-horizon task success, while reducing the data needed for cross-embodiment transfer to a different robot by 10x.
hero_caption: Overview of representative tasks and scale of the FineART dataset. Comprising 40,543 episodes, 1,718 hours, and 533,913 subtasks, it covers not only standard pick-and-place but also contact-rich, long-tail tasks such as deformable object manipulation, tool use, cable routing, and high-precision insertion.
overview:
For robots to execute long-horizon tasks like preparing breakfast or tidying up in the real world, they must coordinate both arms while decomposing the workflow into multiple steps. However, existing single-arm datasets mostly consist of short, single-step actions, and even among bimanual datasets, only a tiny fraction are densely annotated at the subtask level. As a result, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models easily lose track of where they are during multi-minute, complex operations.

To overcome this, the authors built FineART, a large-scale bimanual dataset with human-verified dense subtask annotations across all 1,718 hours and 40,543 episodes (533,913 subtasks in total, averaging about 13 per episode). Furthermore, extending the open-source VLA foundation model $\pi_{0.5}$, they developed FineART-VLA, a unified policy that performs both planning (predicting the next subtask in language) and action execution (continuous joint trajectory generation via Flow Matching). To prevent continuous action loss gradients from corrupting language representations, they introduced Knowledge Insulation (gradient stopping).

Evaluations on physical ALOHA robots showed that subtask training boosted the success rate on a spatial disambiguation task from 32.0% to 100.0%, and lifted success on an unseen long-horizon task under step-by-step human guidance from 16.0% to 76.0%. Moreover, in cross-embodiment adaptation to the mobile bimanual robot YAM—which has a completely different arm configuration—fine-tuning on just five simple tasks required only one-tenth the data of baseline models without mid-training, and enabled zero-shot completion of completely unseen long-horizon tasks (such as breakfast preparation) on the new hardware.
contributions: Built and open-sourced FineART, the largest bimanual manipulation dataset to date, featuring 100% subtask annotation coverage across all 1,718 hours and 40,543 episodes.

Proposed FineART-VLA, unifying linguistic next-subtask prediction and Flow Matching continuous action generation within a single model, incorporating Knowledge Insulation to prevent representation collapse.
Empirically demonstrated on physical hardware that dense subtask training dramatically enhances spatial grounding and performance on unseen long-horizon tasks.

Showed that mid-training a pre-trained VLA on FineART reduces the data required to adapt to a robot with different kinematics and configuration by 10x, enabling zero-shot transfer to unlearned multi-step compound tasks.

sections.heading: Why Do Bimanual Robots Need Dense Subtask Annotations?
sections.summary: Executing multi-minute, long-horizon bimanual tasks requires decomposing work into fine-grained subtasks just like humans do. However, existing datasets mostly focus on single-instruction simple tasks, lacking continuous subtask annotations across long-duration bimanual operations. This paper breaks through this bottleneck with FineART, a dataset with dense subtask labels across all trajectories, and FineART-VLA, a single unified policy trained on it.
sections.details:
Real-world robot tasks like preparing breakfast or putting away tools are long-horizon endeavors requiring intricate coordination between two arms over several minutes. When humans perform such complex tasks, they intuitively break them down into a sequence of subtasks, such as 'pick up plate', 'grasp bread', and 'place bread on plate'. Teaching robots to perform this same feat requires not only long-horizon bimanual operational data itself, but also densely recorded language labels marking subtask boundaries and contents.

However, existing large-scale datasets predominantly feature short single-arm pick-and-place trajectories, each tied to a single episode-level instruction. Even in recent bimanual datasets, subtask annotations are restricted to small subsets, and coverage of contact-rich, challenging skills like deformable object manipulation and tool use remains unclear. On the modeling side, flat VLAs that directly predict actions from high-level instructions struggle to track long-horizon progress, whereas hierarchical setups that separate planners from low-level execution policies add substantial system complexity.

To resolve this, the authors introduce FineART, a dataset containing human-verified subtask annotations across all 1,718 hours and 40,543 episodes (533,913 subtasks in total). They then developed FineART-VLA, which incorporates these annotations as supervision for autoregressive language prediction, unifying reasoning and execution within a single model.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Large Datasets and Hierarchical Policies
sections.summary: Robot learning datasets have scaled up from single-arm to bimanual systems, yet none had dense subtask annotations across all long-horizon bimanual actions. In policy design, unlike hierarchical approaches that split into two separate models or flat models that output actions directly, this work adopts a Chain-of-Thought style approach that unifies planning and action generation inside a single model.
sections.details:
Throughout the history of robot learning, data scaling has progressed across several waves.

### 2.1 Large-Scale Robot Learning Datasets
Beginning with early single-arm teleoperation datasets, open datasets such as Bridge V2 and DROID emerged at scales of tens of thousands to millions of trajectories. However, these remained dominated by short single-arm pick-and-place tasks, almost always pairing a single coarse instruction with an entire episode. Later, affordable bimanual teleoperation systems like ALOHA, multimodal datasets with tactile or audio data, and recent efforts like ABC-130K and MolmoAct2 (Bimanual YAM) advanced the bimanual frontier. Yet, even in ABC-130K, subtask annotations were limited to a subset (1,552 hours). No bimanual long-horizon dataset previously offered dense annotations across its entire duration.

### 2.2 Data Curation and Annotation Pipelines
Dense temporal video annotation originated in video captioning, but in robotics, prior work mostly focused on coarse labeling of play data or dynamically segmenting subtasks online during inference. FineART differs fundamentally by providing consistent, fixed ground-truth subtask labels across all trajectories upfront rather than generating them dynamically at test time.

### 2.3 Language-Conditioned Policies
Most VLA models adopt a flat architecture that outputs actions directly from images and language instructions. However, this causes performance degradation on multi-minute, long-horizon tasks because the model cannot track its own progress. To address this, many prior works adopted hierarchical designs that separate a high-level VLM subtask planner from a low-level execution policy. In contrast, this paper takes an approach akin to Chain-of-Thought, balancing linguistic subtask reasoning and continuous action generation inside a single Flow Matching-based model.

sections.heading: FineART: 1,718 Hours of Fully Annotated Bimanual Data
sections.summary: FineART is a bimanual teleoperation dataset spanning 151 tasks, 40,543 episodes, and 1,718 total hours. Every episode is paired with unconstrained human-annotated subtask labels, comprehensively covering not only standard pick-and-place but also challenging, contact-rich long-tail skills and rich object diversity.
sections.details:
FineART is the world's largest densely subtask-annotated bimanual robot dataset, comprising 40,543 episodes (1,718 hours, approximately 185.5 million frames) across 151 task varieties.

### 3.1 Data Collection Protocol
Hardware data was collected via human teleoperation using an opposed-arm Trossen Stationary ALOHA system (1kg payload ALOHA2 grippers, 50Hz control rate, 300Hz joint telemetry). The camera setup includes four Intel RealSense D405 cameras (30fps, 1280x720): top-down (overhead), worm's-eye (low-angle view capturing contact surfaces), and two wrist-mounted views.
To ensure label quality, an independent dedicated team of human annotators—separate from teleoperators—annotated subtasks in natural language without relying on VLMs, followed by quality audits via statistical sampling from a third-party audit team. Annotations follow a two-tier structure: an episode-level 'Demonstration Label' describing the overall goal, and unconstrained, continuous 'Subtask Labels' that partition time with zero temporal gaps.

### 3.2 Dataset Composition: Long Multistage Tasks
Episodes average 13.17 subtasks each, with a median episode duration of approximately 2.0 minutes, including numerous long-horizon episodes exceeding 10 minutes.

### 3.2.1 Subtask Composition
While 77.2% (1,326.2 hours) of the dataset consists of foundational spatial operations like general pick-and-place (572.7 hours) and semantic tidying (753.5 hours), the remaining 22.8% (391.8 hours) intentionally covers contact-rich 'long-tail skills'. These include deformable object manipulation like folding cloth (126.0 hours), tool-based assembly (111.9 hours), cable routing (59.4 hours), compliant alignment (50.8 hours), and precision mechanical insertion (43.7 hours). Compared to ABC-130K, the median subtask duration is 8.6 seconds (versus 3.5 seconds in ABC-130K), roughly 2.5 times longer, capturing meaningful composite stages beyond atomic grasping and releasing.

### 3.2.2 Object Diversity
To ensure object variety, each task-operator pair was assigned a distinct set of objects every 5 episodes, with placements and orientations randomized every run. A rule-based syntactic parser identified 657 distinct object classes, demonstrating broader diversity than ABC-130K across food, clothing, containers, tools, electronics, and household goods.

### 3.2.3 Descriptive Specificity
The annotations feature high descriptive specificity. Color modifiers appear in 81.1% of subtasks (under 0.01% in ABC-130K), and spatial modifiers appear in 14.8% (0.80% in ABC-130K). Even when multiple identical objects are present, the text uniquely identifies which target to manipulate 81.4% of the time.

captions.F3: An example of FineART's annotation structure. Beneath the high-level demonstration label for the entire episode (orange), continuous, non-overlapping subtask descriptions (blue) partition the trajectory with no gaps, showing how the long-horizon task is broken down step by step.

sections.heading: Dramatic Performance Gains and Cross-Embodiment Transfer from Subtask Training
sections.summary: Mid-training a VLA foundation model on FineART was evaluated across 3,400 physical rollouts on both ALOHA and the different robot YAM. Combining dense subtask learning with Knowledge Insulation proved decisive for spatial grounding and long-horizon success, while demonstrating remarkable transfer to unseen hardware and tasks.
sections.details:
Experiments used the pre-trained generalist VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$ as a base, conducting 300,000 steps of mid-training on FineART (equivalent to roughly 10% of the full dataset). Physical hardware evaluations totaled 3,400 rollouts.

### 4.1 Policy and Mid-Training Setup
FineART-VLA consists of a 2B-parameter Gemma language backbone, a SigLIP vision encoder, and a 300M-parameter Gemma-style action expert. Inputs include three camera views (overhead and both wrists) along with a 14-dimensional joint and gripper state. The model predicts the next subtask text string, a discrete tokenized action sequence $	ilde{a}$, and a 50-step continuous action chunk $A_t$. The loss is the sum of the Flow Matching loss ($\lambda_{	ext{flow}}=10$), discrete token loss ($\lambda_{	ext{fast}}=1$), and text generation loss ($\lambda_{	ext{text}}\in\{0,1\}$).
Crucially, the architecture incorporates 'Knowledge Insulation (KI)'. By applying a stop-gradient between the newly attached action expert and the VLM backbone, gradients from continuous action learning do not backpropagate into the VLM, preventing the degradation of its pre-trained visual and linguistic representations.

### 4.2 In-Embodiment Results (ALOHA)
On the same ALOHA hardware used for collection, policies were evaluated across 25 strictly defined initial object configurations per task.

- **OOD Generalization and KI Impact**: Comparing models with and without subtask training and KI, the variant enabling both achieved the highest generalization to unseen tasks.
- **Importance of Long-Tail Data**: Removing the contact-rich long-tail tasks (22.8% of the data) during mid-training caused average success to plummet from 24.7% to 14.0%. Beyond category coverage, skill diversity in challenging manipulation directly drives overall generalization.
- **Spatial Grounding**: On a spatial disambiguation task ('put the donut in the [left / right / middle] bin'), the policy without subtask training achieved only 32.0% (with all failures caused by placing into incorrect bins), whereas the subtask-trained policy achieved 100.0% success.
- **Long-Horizon Tracking**: On an unseen multi-stage 'breakfast preparation' task, while full autonomous execution failed, providing step-by-step human guidance upon step completion lifted success from 16.0% (without subtask training) to 76.0% with subtask training.
- **Emergent Recovery Behaviors**: The model exhibited sophisticated closed-loop behaviors that were never explicitly demonstrated, such as self-correction (retracting an arm heading toward the wrong bin), failure recovery (re-grasping a dropped cup), and bimanual coordination (stabilizing a vase with the left hand while inserting a flower with the right).

### 4.3 Cross-Embodiment Transfer (YAM)
In a more demanding test, the policy was transferred from ALOHA's opposed-arm setup to YAM, a mobile bimanual robot with forward-facing arms. The best ALOHA-mid-trained checkpoint was fine-tuned for just 5,000 steps on 5 simple tasks on YAM.

- **Data Efficiency**: While a baseline without mid-training required 250 episodes per task, FineART-VLA surpassed it with only 25 episodes, achieving a 26.4% success rate and cutting required data by 10x.
- **Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Long-Horizon Tasks**: Most remarkably, on a breakfast preparation task (place plate on tray, arrange two buns and bread) that was completely absent from YAM's fine-tuning data, FineART-VLA achieved a 28.0% success rate and 78.3% progress rate via autonomous hierarchical reasoning. Furthermore, it spontaneously generated and executed an 'Adjust tray' subtask that existed only in ALOHA data and had never been demonstrated on YAM. This indicates that high-level task structure planning transfers across robot embodiments, while minimal downstream fine-tuning data grounds the specific kinematics of the new hardware.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Horizons
sections.summary: FineART is the first open bimanual dataset with dense subtask annotations across 100% of its data, and the resulting VLA model delivers tremendous benefits in spatial reasoning, long-horizon task execution, and cross-embodiment transfer. Future avenues include longer training horizons, subtask-conditioned world models, and reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
This work introduced FineART, an open dataset spanning 40,543 episodes and 1,718 hours with 533,913 subtask annotations, alongside FineART-VLA, which unifies self-subtask prediction and continuous action generation in a single policy. Experimental results confirm that mid-training with dense subtask labels and Knowledge Insulation yields robust OOD generalization, precise spatial instruction following, long-horizon step execution, and dramatic data savings with zero-shot transfer to completely different robot embodiments.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors highlight several limitations and future research directions:
- **Single Collection Platform**: All demonstration data was collected on a single hardware setup, Stationary ALOHA.
- **Compute Constraints**: Due to resource limits, policy training covered only roughly 10% of the dataset (0.1 epochs, 300k steps); evaluating longer training runs and alternative backbones remains necessary.
- **Future Extensions**: Promising directions include subtask-conditioned world models, reward models, and advantage-conditioned reinforcement learning from failure trajectories. Additionally, automating subtask labeling with VLMs will be vital to reduce annotation costs as datasets scale further.

sections.heading: Appendix: Architecture Details, Sampling Strategy, and Evaluation Protocols
sections.summary: This section covers the internal model architecture, temperature-based task sampling to resolve data imbalance, mathematical formulation of Knowledge Insulation, and the 25-condition physical evaluation protocol ensuring reproducibility.
sections.details:
### A.1 Task-Balanced Sampling
The 151 tasks in FineART vary widely in volume, from dozens to thousands of episodes. Uniformly sampling frames would overfit large tasks. The authors therefore adopt temperature-scaled sampling where task sampling probability is proportional to $n_i^\alpha$ (with $\alpha=0.5$), where $n_i$ is the number of valid frames. This tempers the disparity between task sizes and ensures sufficient gradient steps for smaller, long-tail tasks.

### A.2 Mathematics of Knowledge Insulation
When the action expert layers attend to the Key/Value representations of the VLM backbone, a stop-gradient operator $\mathrm{sg}(\cdot)$ is applied. In the forward pass, values pass through unchanged, but in the backward pass, gradients are zeroed out. As a result, gradients from the Flow Matching loss $\mathcal{L}_{	ext{flow}}$ to the VLM backbone weights $	heta_{	ext{VLM}}$ are identically zero. This preserves the general language and visual features acquired during pre-training.

### B.1 & B.2 Evaluation Procedure
To ensure evaluation rigor and reproducibility, 25 standardized initial object positions and orientations (Initial Conditions) were defined for each benchmark evaluation task. Every model checkpoint was evaluated from these identical initial states.

captions.F12: The 25 initial configurations used for the evaluation task 'put cup on shelf'. Evaluating all model checkpoints from these exact initial conditions minimizes rollout variance and ensures fair, rigorous comparisons.

takeaways: In long-horizon manipulation, dense linguistic subtask annotations—not just raw trajectory data—dramatically improve a model's progress tracking and spatial grounding.
When attaching a continuous action head to a pre-trained VLM, protecting the language backbone via Knowledge Insulation (gradient stopping) is essential for out-of-distribution generalization.
Incorporating contact-rich, long-tail skills (cloth manipulation, tool use, precision insertion) elevates overall policy generalization across all tasks, including basic pick-and-place.

Mid-training on high-quality subtask-annotated data allows policies to adapt to robots with fundamentally different kinematics using minimal fine-tuning, transferring high-level task structure zero-shot.
limitations: All trajectory data was collected on a single hardware platform (Stationary ALOHA), offering no morphological diversity during the initial collection phase.
Due to compute constraints, the policy was trained on only about 10% of the 1,718-hour dataset (roughly 0.1 epochs, 300k steps).
Because all dense subtask annotations were generated manually by human experts, lowering annotation costs (e.g., via VLM automation) will be crucial for future dataset expansions.
